title: 3 Days in Istanbul: What You Actually Have to See
titleTag: 3 Days in Istanbul: The Must-See Itinerary
ogTitle: 3 Days in Istanbul — The Must-See Itinerary
metaDescription: The essential three-day Istanbul itinerary: Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapi and the bazaars, ordered around the closures that break most plans.

standfirst: Three days is enough for Istanbul's essentials, but only if you build the plan around the closures. Here is what genuinely has to be on the list, ordered so you never walk up to a locked door.
cardSummary: Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapi and the bazaars — what to see and what to skip.

heroImage.alt: Hagia Sophia's grey dome, buttresses and four minarets seen from across Sultanahmet
heroImage.caption: Hagia Sophia. Fifteen centuries of cathedral, mosque and museum, and it still dominates the skyline it was built for.

body: Three days covers Istanbul's essentials comfortably: the two great mosques and the cistern in Sultanahmet, Topkapi and the bazaars, and Galata with a ferry across to the Asian side. What it does not cover is the Bosphorus villages or the Princes' Islands, both of which need a full day and are the things most three-day itineraries wrongly try to squeeze in.

Almost nothing here is far from anything else. Sultanahmet is walkable end to end, and the tram covers the rest. What ruins days in Istanbul is not distance. It is arriving at a door that is shut, and the city shuts a lot of doors on a schedule most itineraries ignore.

**Check which weekdays your trip covers before you fix anything.** Topkapi Palace closes on Tuesdays. The Grand Bazaar closes on Sundays. Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque are working mosques and stop admitting visitors at each of the five daily prayers, with the long closure around midday on Friday. Fit the plan to those holes first and fill in the rest afterwards.

sections.heading: Day 1 — Sultanahmet and the prayer clock
body: Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque face each other across a park, about two minutes apart. Both stop admitting visitors while prayers are held, and not at quite the same moments. So the move is simple. Get there early, go into whichever one is open, and cross to the other afterwards.

Know what you are buying at Hagia Sophia. Since it returned to use as a mosque, foreign visitors are routed to the upper gallery on a paid ticket rather than walking the main floor. It is still worth it for the mosaics and the scale of the dome, but arrive expecting a gallery visit. The Blue Mosque, across the park, is free.

**Dress for it and you will not be stopped.** Shoulders and knees covered, for everyone, and a headscarf for women. Shoes come off at the door of a working mosque. Scarves are usually available at the entrance, but bringing your own saves a queue.

sections.alt: The domes and six minarets of the Blue Mosque above the trees of Sultanahmet Park in late afternoon light
sections.caption: The Blue Mosque from Sultanahmet Park. Six minarets, no ticket, and the same prayer-time closures as its neighbour.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: All within a few minutes of each other. The order depends on which mosque is admitting visitors when you arrive.

stops.name: Hagia Sophia
stops.detail: Go at opening, and not around midday on a Friday. Foreign visitors see it from the upper gallery on a paid ticket, which is where the surviving mosaics are anyway.

stops.name: Blue Mosque
stops.detail: Two minutes across the park, and free. If prayers have just started, walk the Hippodrome first and come back.

stops.name: The Hippodrome
stops.detail: The old chariot track, now a long public square with an Egyptian obelisk still standing where the Romans put it. Ten minutes, no ticket.

stops.name: Basilica Cistern
stops.detail: A sunken Roman reservoir of lit columns under the street. Book online: the door queue runs long through the warm months and the visit itself is short.

stops.name: Sultanahmet at dusk
stops.detail: The mosques are lit after dark and the day-trip crowds have gone. Come back after dinner. It is a different square.

sections.heading: Day 2 — Topkapi, Suleymaniye and the bazaars
body: This is the day with two closures in it, so it moves if it has to. Topkapi shuts on Tuesdays and the Grand Bazaar shuts on Sundays. If your middle day lands on either, swap this with Day 3 and nothing else changes.

Topkapi is large and easy to underestimate. Give it a full morning, and buy the Harem as well, which is a separate ticket and the part most worth the extra. Last admission falls earlier than the closing time, so an afternoon arrival is a bad plan even on an open day.

Between the palace and the bazaar, stop at Suleymaniye. It is Sinan's masterpiece, it sits on a terrace with the best open view over the Golden Horn, and it carries a fraction of the crowd that Sultanahmet does. Most three-day lists leave it out, which is their mistake.

sections.alt: A painted vaulted arcade inside the Grand Bazaar with jewellery shops along both sides and several shutters closed
sections.caption: Inside the Grand Bazaar. The painted vaults are the reason to look up, and half-closed shutters are what you get if you time it wrong.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: Not a Tuesday, and not a Sunday. Everything below runs gently downhill towards the water.

stops.name: Topkapi Palace
stops.detail: Closed Tuesdays. Courtyards, treasury and the view over the Bosphorus from the terrace. Add the Harem ticket and allow longer than you think.

stops.name: Suleymaniye Mosque
stops.detail: Sinan's best building, on a terrace above the Golden Horn. Quieter than anything in Sultanahmet and free to enter.

stops.name: Grand Bazaar
stops.detail: Closed Sundays. Go for the painted vaults and the sheer scale of it rather than for the shopping, which is mostly aimed at you.

stops.name: Spice Bazaar
stops.detail: Downhill from the Grand Bazaar and open every day, including the Sunday the other one is shut. Smaller, louder, better for food.

stops.name: Galata Bridge
stops.detail: Anglers stand shoulder to shoulder along the rail on the upper deck, with fish restaurants packed in underneath them. Walk out as the light goes.

sections.heading: Day 3 — Galata, Beyoglu and the ferry to Asia
body: Cross the Golden Horn. Galata and Beyoglu are the nineteenth-century city, steeper and denser than Sultanahmet, and the walk up from the bridge to the tower is the sharpest climb of the trip.

Then get on a ferry. A public Sehir Hatlari ferry to Kadikoy or Uskudar takes an Istanbulkart tap, runs on a published timetable, and crosses exactly the same water as the cruise boats selling tickets on the quay. There is no commentary and no complimentary tea, which is the entire difference in exchange for a fraction of the price.

sections.alt: A white passenger ferry crossing the Golden Horn in front of the Galata Bridge, with Galata Tower on the hill behind
sections.caption: A public ferry crossing in front of the Galata Bridge. This is the same water the cruise boats sell tickets for.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: Uphill first, then the water. Save the crossing for the end of the afternoon and come back into the sunset.

stops.name: Galata Tower
stops.detail: The view is genuinely good and the queue is genuinely long. If it is backed up round the block, the same panorama is free from the ferry deck later.

stops.name: Istiklal Caddesi
stops.detail: The long pedestrian spine of Beyoglu, with the red heritage tram grinding down the middle of it. Duck into the side passages for lunch.

stops.name: Ferry to Kadikoy
stops.detail: Tap an Istanbulkart and sit outside. Twenty minutes of the skyline from the water, for the price of a bus fare.

stops.name: Kadikoy market streets
stops.detail: This is where the city eats when nobody is watching. Denser than anything across the water, cheaper too, and almost nobody on the street is a tourist.

stops.name: The ferry back
stops.detail: Time the return for sunset. The old city comes at you in silhouette, minaret by minaret, and it costs nothing extra.

rows: Move the palace day. Do Suleymaniye and the bazaars instead
The Spice Bazaar is open. Swap the bazaar day for Galata

Free, and two minutes from the last one

sections.heading: What three days does not cover
sections.intro: Cutting deliberately beats rushing. These need more time than you have:
items: **The Bosphorus villages** — Ortakoy, Bebek and the fortress up the strait are a full day on the water.
**The Princes' Islands** — a ferry each way and a car-free afternoon. Worth it, and not on this trip.
**Dolmabahce Palace** — a half day, and a completely different century from Topkapi.
**The Chora church** — the finest Byzantine mosaics in the city, and awkwardly far out west.
**The Asian side beyond Kadikoy** — Moda, Uskudar and the coast road deserve their own morning.

faqHeading: Common questions about 3 days in Istanbul

faq.a: For the essentials, yes. Three days covers Sultanahmet, Topkapi and the bazaars, and Galata with a ferry to the Asian side. It is not enough to add the Bosphorus villages or the Princes' Islands, each of which needs a day of its own.

faq.q: What are the must-see sights in Istanbul?
faq.a: Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapi Palace and the Grand Bazaar are the four nobody should miss. Suleymaniye Mosque is the strongest addition after those, and it is quieter and better sited than anything in Sultanahmet.

faq.q: Which days are things closed in Istanbul?
faq.a: Topkapi Palace closes on Tuesdays and the Grand Bazaar closes on Sundays. The Spice Bazaar and the Basilica Cistern open daily. Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque are working mosques that pause visits at each of the five daily prayers, with the longest closure around midday on Friday.

faq.q: Can you visit Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque on the same day?
faq.a: Easily. They face each other across a park about two minutes apart. Because each stops admitting visitors at its own prayer times, go early and start with whichever is open, then cross to the other. Avoid the middle of Friday for both.

faq.q: What should I wear to visit the mosques?
faq.a: Shoulders and knees covered, for men and women, plus a headscarf for women. Shoes come off at the door. Scarves are usually available at the entrance, though bringing your own avoids another queue.

faq.q: Is a Bosphorus cruise worth it?
faq.a: Not the ticketed kind, on a three-day trip. A public ferry to Kadikoy or Uskudar costs an Istanbulkart tap and crosses the same water with the same views. What you lose is the narration and the tea; what you save is most of the afternoon and most of the money.

faq.q: How do you get around Istanbul?
faq.a: Trams and ferries, both on an Istanbulkart. The T1 tram runs through Sultanahmet and over the Galata Bridge, which covers most of this itinerary, and the ferries handle the crossings. Buy the card at any station machine and top it up as you go.
